planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Frederick is a purple-fruited passionfruit selected for vigor and reliable production.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Frederick is a vigorous purple-fruited passionfruit cultivar valued for heavy production of aromatic, tart-sweet fruit on fast-growing vines. Like other purple passionfruit types it fruits within the first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant, considerably faster than seed-grown vines, and ripe fruit drops naturally from the vine when ready to pick. Vines are vigorous climbers and need sturdy support along with regular tip-pruning to keep growth directed and manageable rather than sprawling. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily going into winter, since purple passionfruit types are more cold-sensitive than the hardier Possum Purple selection and a hard freeze can kill the vine to the ground or outright.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Passionfruit Production

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Nellie Kelly is a widely planted purple passionfruit selected for disease tolerance and reliable heavy cropping.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Nellie Kelly is a purple passionfruit cultivar popular in Australian and subtropical home gardens for its combination of good disease resistance, heavy cropping, and rich, tangy flavor. The vine grows quickly and begins fruiting within its first year, producing abundant deep-purple fruit that drop naturally from the vine when ripe. Give the vigorous vine a sturdy trellis or fence and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage lateral branching, which increases the fruiting wood. In zone 9, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden and mulch heavily over winter, since purple passionfruit types tolerate cold less well than the hardier Possum Purple hybrid and can be killed back or outright by a hard freeze.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Passionfruit Production

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Panama Red is a large-fruited purple-red passionfruit selection popular for fresh eating and juice.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Red is a purple-red-skinned passionfruit selection valued for producing larger fruit than many standard purple passionfruit types, with rich, aromatic, tart-sweet pulp well suited to both fresh eating and juicing. The vigorous vine climbs quickly and begins bearing within its first year from a rooted cutting, dropping ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to harvest. Provide sturdy support and pinch new growth periodically to keep the vine directing energy into fruiting wood rather than unchecked vegetative sprawl. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily each winter, since this cultivar shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden

planting.note: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter; Smooth Cayenne is the classic commercial pineapple, needing about 18-24 months from planting to fruit.

directions: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Smooth Cayenne is the classic commercial pineapple cultivar grown throughout the tropics for its large, cylindrical, juicy, sweet-tart fruit with relatively smooth, spineless leaf margins that make handling far easier than older spiny pineapple types. Plants form a low rosette of stiff, strap-like leaves and take 18-24 months from planting to produce a single fruit at the center of the rosette, after which side suckers can be removed and replanted to start new plants. Because pineapple has essentially no frost tolerance, zone 9 gardeners should grow it in a large container that can be moved to a greenhouse, garage, or bright indoor spot before the first freeze, bringing it back outside once nights stay reliably above 50F. Full sun, warmth, and free-draining soil or potting mix are the main requirements for good fruit size and flavor.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pineapple Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pineapple Production

planting.note: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter; Red Spanish is an older heirloom pineapple valued for its tough skin and good shipping and storage qualities.

directions: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Red Spanish is an heirloom pineapple cultivar with a squat, barrel-shaped fruit and tough reddish-orange skin that historically made it a favorite for shipping and fresh market sale before modern refrigerated transport, since the thick rind resists bruising and handling damage. Flesh is pale yellow, firm, and tangy-sweet with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving alike. Like other pineapples, the low rosette of stiff, often spiny leaves takes about 18-24 months to mature a single fruit at its center, after which offset suckers can be detached and replanted. Pineapple has virtually no cold tolerance, so zone 9 gardeners should grow Red Spanish in a large container that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse before the first freeze and returned outside once nights stay reliably above 50F.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pineapple Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pineapple Production
